newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Speaking freely.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Speaking freely.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)

John Howard rushed back from Tokyo overnight last Friday - half a day early - to honour a speaking engagement at the Liberal Party's Queensland state conference, an appropriate venue, he thought, to dally with the Pauline Hanson issue.
It must be quickly pointed out that her name was never mentioned.
But it may as well have been flashing lights so palpable was her aura on the gathering.
She would have been there had she not made one of her controversial statements before the last election which earned her immediate expulsion from the Liberal Party.
It's now history, of course, that she continued to stand for the seat of Oxley, centred on the Queensland city of Ipswich, winning it handsomely as an independent.
Then a little over two weeks ago Hanson took her place in the spotlight with the now famous/notorious maiden speech.
Politicians of all colours have been running from it ever since, like Dracula from the stake.
The reason is not hard to fathom.
The content of the speech was long on ignorance, unreality and -- this is the dangerous part -- populism.

Talk-back radio is still dominated by views for and against (mostly for) and the letters pages of the newspapers have at least two or three a day, although the Hanson letters are still rolling in at a rate sufficient to fill these pages on any given day.
Kim Beazley has struggled to a position.
This week Beazley said: "I mean she's an independent member, she's just arrived."
"The question for us in political parties is how you devise a policy that ensures the health and survival of the nation," Beazley said.
"And she's not exactly in that debate," he said.
But the prime minister is more cagey.
His strategy was not to confront it until public opinion was clearer.
Then in the Queensland speech to deal with it in the abstract.
Hence the 'freedom of expression' speech; the claims that the yoke of political correctness had been lifted in the six months since he took office; that people now felt free to speak their minds.
Neither stands up to much serious scrutiny.
His rider that this new freedom brought with it the responsibility to use it wisely and fairly was widely interpreted as a shot at Hanson.
Wrong, said Howard.
"That speech had nothing to do with Pauline Hanson," he said.
On Channel Nine's Current Affair programme Howard was boasting about the tolerance of the Liberal Party.
Interviewer Ray Martin shot back: "The Liberal Party wasn't so tolerant of Pauline Hanson before the election. Did you agree with kicking her out?"
Answer: "Yes."
Question: "Would you have her back in the party now with what she said?"
Answer: "Well, she's not interested in coming back and I don't think the issue arises."
It was all a bit hesitant, in contrast to the more forceful tone he used earlier when discussing his meeting with the Dalai Lama.
It was also clear that no-one really believes this speech wasn't about Pauline Hanson, at least on the periphery.
But it should also have become clear to the prime minister and his advisers that this sort of thing is tantamount to playing with fire.
Political leaders have long realised that you can't just put a toe in the water of the debate over race and multiculturalism and then retreat to higher ground.
But Howard never really got over the furore and the aftermath which erupted around his 1988 comments suggesting Asian immigration should be cut back.
Although bound up with other leadership issues, the immigration comment was the catalyst which led to a deeper questioning of Howard's leadership of the Opposition at that point.
Victorian Liberals, in particular, used it as a rallying point to begin a destabilisation in favour of Victoria's favourite Liberal, Andrew Peacock.
Howard later apologised for the 1988 remarks but the whole issue has burned within ever since.
It's now re-emerging in his regular comments against so-called political correctness and now his view about the new freedom of expression abroad in the land.

But almost immediately came the backlash, first in the form of a rash of newspaper features and editorials disputing his claim and then in more practical terms with the announcement by the eccentric British historian David Irving that he would now reapply for a visa to visit Australia to promote his views questioning the holocaust.
Irving has been knocked back under the former government, with support from the then Opposition.
There's no record of Howard having supported his previous applications.

Howard denounced the Irving announcement as gimmickry and will doubtless avoid serious controversy by allowing the application to be dealt with under the current law and regulations which is almost certain to once again rule him out.
Gimmick or not, Irving's action was a warning to all politicians of the dangers of trying to catch the occasional wave of public opinion.
They can turn into dumpers.
(Views are those of the author, not those of Reuters)
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
